hero.title: Protecting community cats in Orihuela Costa.
hero.lead: We are neighbours from Orihuela Costa who look after the local cat colonies every single day. With the TNR method (trap, neuter, return) colonies stop growing, cats live healthier lives and the neighbourhood becomes a calmer place.
hero.earTitle: Spotted a cat with a clipped ear tip?
hero.earText: It means the cat has been neutered, checked by a vet and is protected as part of a managed colony.
hero.sceneLabel: Illustration: three cats sitting on a wall facing the sea at sunset. One of them has a clipped ear tip.

work.title: Caring for a colony is much more than leaving food out
work.lead: Every colony has its own volunteers who know each cat individually. This is our daily work:

items.title: Feeding and cleaning
items.text: Dry food and fresh water at fixed spots and times. We always clean up afterwards so no mess or leftovers are left behind.

items.title: Neutering with TNR
items.text: We trap humanely, take each cat to the vet and return it to its colony. It's the only way to stop the population from growing.

items.title: Health monitoring
items.text: We keep a census of every colony and watch for injuries, illness and newcomers so they get veterinary care in time.

items.title: Neighbours and regulations
items.text: We mediate with residents and communities, make sure the law is respected and work with the Town Council to have colonies officially recognised.

steps.title: The TNR method in three steps
steps.lead: It's the method set out in Spain's national animal welfare law for managing cat colonies, and the one we use across the whole of Orihuela Costa.

items.title: Trap
items.text: Using approved humane traps, without harming the animal and with as little stress as possible.

items.title: Neuter
items.text: A vet neuters, deworms and checks the cat, and clips the tip of one ear to identify it.

items.title: Return
items.text: Once recovered, the cat goes back to its colony, where we keep caring for it for the rest of its life.

steps.link: All about TNR and the law

benefits.title: A cared-for colony is good for the whole neighbourhood
benefits.lead: Community cats are part of the urban ecosystem. Well managed, they give back more than most people imagine.

items.title: Fewer rodents
items.text: Their presence alone keeps rats and mice from settling in gardens, empty plots and shared areas.

items.title: Quieter nights
items.text: Without mating seasons, night-time yowling, fights and urine marking disappear.

items.title: A population that stops growing
items.text: Neutered cats hold their territory and don't reproduce, so no new litters arrive.

items.title: Better public health
items.text: These cats are checked by vets, monitored, and fed at clean feeding points.

items.title: Lower public spending
items.text: Neutering once costs less than removing litters year after year without ever solving the problem.

items.title: Community
items.text: Caring for those without a voice brings neighbours together and teaches children respect.

law.title: Since 2023, the law protects them
law.text: Spain's Law 7/2023 on the protection of animal rights and welfare recognises community cats and requires town councils to manage cat colonies using the TNR method. It is no longer a matter of goodwill: it's a legal obligation.

volunteer.metaDescription: Find out what it means to volunteer with Cats Ocosta: give your time to the cat colonies of Orihuela Costa or support us with donations.
volunteer.title: Become a volunteer
volunteer.lead: You don't need experience or to be a vet. You need commitment, respect for animals and for neighbours, and a wish to work as a team.
volunteer.meaningTitle: What it means to volunteer with Cats Ocosta
meaning: Volunteering means committing to cats who have nobody else. Colonies need food and water every day of the year, including August and Christmas, and that is only possible if many of us share the work.

It also means representing the association to local residents: explaining what we do, why the colony is there and how it makes the neighbourhood better. Every volunteer helps change how people see community cats.

volunteer.commitTitle: What we ask of every volunteer

commit.title: Coordination
commit.text: We always act on behalf of the association and with the approval of each area's coordinator.

commit.title: Cleanliness
commit.text: Clearing bowls and leftovers after every feed. It's what neighbours appreciate most.

commit.title: Discretion
commit.text: We never share the exact location of colonies, to protect them from abandonment and attacks.

commit.title: Respect
commit.text: For the cats, for the neighbours and for local regulations.

faq.q: Do I have to live in Orihuela Costa?
faq.a: For colony volunteering it helps to live nearby, since shifts are daily. If you live further away you can help with donations, sharing our posts or one-off campaigns.

faq.q: How much time do I need to give?
faq.a: A feeding shift usually takes 30 to 60 minutes. What matters most isn't the number of hours but consistency: if you commit to one day a week, the cats count on it.

faq.q: Can I help if I'm under 18?
faq.a: Yes, accompanied by an adult and with your parents' or guardians' permission. Some tasks, like information stands, are a great way to start.

faq.q: I already feed some cats on my own. What should I do?
faq.a: Get in touch. We'll help get that colony neutered and registered, and make sure feeding follows local regulations. That way the cats are protected, and so are you.

faq.q: What should I do if I find a kitten or an injured cat?
faq.a: Message us on WhatsApp with a photo and the approximate area. If the animal is in immediate danger, take it to an emergency vet.

tnr.metaTitle: The TNR method and community cats' rights
tnr.metaDescription: What the TNR method (trap, neuter, return) is, why it works, what Spain's Law 7/2023 says about community cats and how they benefit the community.
tnr.title: The TNR method
tnr.lead: Trap, neuter, return. It's the ethical and effective way to manage colonies of cats living outdoors, and the method set out in Spain's national animal welfare law.

what.title: What the TNR method is
what.text: TNR stands for trap, neuter, return (in Spanish, CER: captura, esterilización y retorno). Every cat in a colony is neutered and returned to its territory, where a team of volunteers feeds them, keeps a census and monitors their health. The colony stops growing and, over the years, shrinks naturally.

steps.title: Trap
steps.text: We use traps designed not to cause harm. They're set at the times cats come to eat and are watched at all times.

steps.title: Neuter
steps.text: At the vet clinic the cat is neutered, dewormed and given a general check-up. Under anaesthesia the tip of one ear is clipped: the international sign of a neutered cat.

steps.title: Return
steps.text: After recovering, the cat goes back to exactly the same spot where it was trapped. Its colony is its home.

steps.title: Follow-up
steps.text: Volunteers keep feeding the colony, record every cat and spot newcomers so they can be neutered too.

why.title: Why it works
why.lead: For decades people tried to solve the problem by removing cats. It never worked. TNR does, for these reasons:

items.title: It breaks the breeding cycle
items.text: A female cat can have several litters a year. Without neutering, a small colony multiplies very quickly.

items.title: It avoids the vacuum effect
items.text: If a colony is removed, food and shelter remain, and other unneutered cats move in. A stable, neutered colony keeps the territory occupied.

items.title: It reduces nuisance
items.text: Without mating cycles, yowling, fighting and urine marking disappear — the main causes of complaints from residents.

items.title: It improves the cats' health
items.text: Neutered cats fight less, roam less and get regular veterinary check-ups.

items.title: It's ethical and backed by law
items.text: It doesn't involve killing healthy animals, and it's the reference method under Law 7/2023.

items.myth: If you feed them, more cats will come.
items.fact: Orderly feeding at fixed times is exactly what makes it possible to trap and neuter the whole colony. What makes a colony grow is breeding, not food.

items.myth: It's best to take them somewhere else.
items.fact: Because of the vacuum effect, other cats would arrive. Besides, the law generally forbids removing or relocating community cats from their colony except in the cases and procedures it sets out.
Cats in a managed colony are checked and dewormed. With basic hygiene, the risk to people is very low.

items.myth: They'd be better off in a home.
items.fact: Most colony cats aren't socialised with people and would suffer indoors. Their territory is their home. Kittens and friendly cats are put up for adoption.

law.title: How the law protects community cats
law.lead: Spain's Law 7/2023, of 28 March, on the protection of animal rights and welfare, in force since 29 September 2023, has a chapter dedicated specifically to cat colonies.

items.title: It recognises the community cat
items.text: It defines a community cat as one that lives freely but is linked to a territory, and a cat colony as a group of cats that, due to low socialisation, can't easily be handled by people but lives around them.

items.title: It sets TNR as the management method
items.text: It defines TNR as the trapping, neutering and return of community cats by non-harmful means, and establishes comprehensive, non-lethal colony management.

items.title: It gives responsibilities to town councils
items.text: Municipalities must run cat colony management programmes including census, neutering and health control, working with animal protection organisations.

items.title: It requires owned cats to be neutered
items.text: To stop new cats ending up on the street, the law requires pet cats to be neutered, with the exceptions it provides for.

items.title: It punishes cruelty
items.text: Abandonment and cruelty are forbidden and penalised. In addition, the Criminal Code, amended in 2023, punishes animal cruelty with penalties that can include prison.

law.regional: In the Valencian Community, Regional Law 2/2023, of 13 March, on the protection, welfare and keeping of companion animals also applies, and each town council sets out in its bylaws how colonies are registered and managed.
law.disclaimer: This information is for general awareness and is not legal advice. You can read the full text of the law in Spain's Official State Gazette (BOE).

rights.title: Community cats' rights today
rights.lead: Under current law, a colony cat has the right to:
items: Live in its territory, without being removed or relocated except in the cases set out by law
Be treated with dignity and not suffer cruelty, poisoning or abandonment
Be fed and cared for by the people and organisations managing its colony
Receive veterinary care and be neutered as part of a TNR programme
Not be put down, except for euthanasia prescribed by a vet to prevent suffering
rights.reportText: Call 112 or 062 (Guardia Civil, SEPRONA) or alert the Local Police. If you can do so safely, take photos or video and note the time and place. Then message us: we'll support you through the report.

items.title: Natural rodent control
items.text: They keep rats and mice away from homes, gardens and shared areas, with no need for poisons that endanger pets and children.

items.title: Calmer coexistence
items.text: A neutered colony doesn't yowl in heat, fight or spray urine.

items.title: Public health
items.text: Managed colonies are under veterinary control and fed at clean feeding points, unlike unmanaged cats.

items.title: Savings for the town
items.text: TNR solves the problem in the long term, which makes it cheaper than repeated removals.

items.title: Teaching values
items.text: Colonies are a chance to teach children and young people respect for animals and for shared spaces.

items.title: Neighbours who know each other
items.text: Around every colony grows a network of people who help one another and look after their surroundings.

p: In accordance with article 10 of Spanish Law 34/2002 on information society services and e-commerce (LSSI-CE), this notice identifies the owner of this website, whose purpose is to present the association's work, explain the TNR method and make it easy to get in touch and collaborate.
Access to this website is free and requires no registration. Visitors agree to make appropriate use of its content, in accordance with the law and good faith.

This website links to third-party services such as Teaming for donations, WhatsApp for contact, and Spain's Official State Gazette. The association is not responsible for their content or privacy policies, which we recommend you read.
This legal notice is governed by Spanish law.

This website has no forms, doesn't let you create accounts, uses no tracking cookies or analytics tools, and stores no personal data about visitors. This policy explains what happens to your data only if you choose to contact us or collaborate.

Like any web server, the hosting provider may technically and temporarily log IP addresses and request data to keep the service secure and working. The association doesn't use these logs to identify you or build profiles.

sections.h: If you email us or message us on WhatsApp
p: We'll process the data you give us (name, phone number or email and the content of your message) solely to reply to you and, if you want to volunteer, to coordinate your involvement. The legal basis is your consent when contacting us and, for volunteering, managing the relationship established with you.
We'll keep your data for as long as needed to handle your enquiry or while you collaborate with the association, and then delete it. We don't share it with third parties unless legally required.

WhatsApp is a service provided by WhatsApp Ireland Limited, which processes your data as an independent controller under its own privacy policy; this may involve international transfers covered by the mechanisms provided for in the GDPR.
Donations are made on the Teaming platform, which is responsible for any data you provide there under its own privacy policy. This website never receives or stores payment details.

You can exercise your rights of access, rectification, erasure, objection, restriction of processing and portability by writing to {email}. If you believe we haven't handled your rights properly, you can lodge a complaint with the Spanish Data Protection Agency (www.aepd.es).
If you're under 14, please ask your parent or guardian to contact us on your behalf.

sections.h: This website uses no tracking cookies
p: We don't use analytics, advertising or social media cookies, and we don't load third-party content that sets them. We don't even store a cookie to remember your language: it's shown in the page address itself (/es or /en). That's why we don't show you a cookie banner.

sections.h: Technical cookie for the admin panel
p: Only team members who publish on the blog access a private panel. Logging in creates a technical cookie (payload-token) required to keep the session open. It is exempt from consent under article 22.2 of the LSSI-CE and is never set for website visitors.
If you click a link to Teaming or WhatsApp you'll leave this website, and those services may use their own cookies under their policies.
You can view and delete cookies from your browser settings at any time.
